notes:
FICTIONAL equal-weight adult cohort, not recovered persons or a fitted reconstruction of the excluded survey. Intended to stand in for the specified peso_lab-weighted complete-case, positive-weight, non-reported-pregnant 20–79 analytical distribution only under transport assumptions. No national representativeness assertion. No HbA1c, treatment, or hypertension restriction is imposed. Selection/pregnancy/laboratory participation are not individually simulated; their effects on the released complete-case distribution are unknown.

Evidence actually retrieved: (1) Brant et al., Relations of digital vascular function, cardiovascular risk factors, and arterial stiffness: ELSA-Brasil, 2014, doi:10.1161/JAHA.114.001279, PMC4338719, Methods and Table 1. 1,535 civil servants aged 35–74 from the Minas Gerais baseline center, 2008–2010, selected for technically usable peripheral arterial tonometry. Marginal mean±SD: age 52±9 years, women 44%, BMI 26.8±4.6 kg/m2, SBP 122±17 and DBP 78±11 mmHg. BP average of second and third of three seated automated readings after five minutes rest. These are reference-population scale anchors, not target summaries. (2) Linderman et al., 2018, doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2018.1271, PMC6324286, Statistical Analysis and Results. China-PEACE convenience screening of 1,727,411 adults aged 35–80, 2014–2017, including treated participants. Observed-pressure BMI coefficients 1.15 SBP and 0.75 DBP mmHg per kg/m2, i.e. 5.75 and 3.75 per 5 kg/m2. The source model adjusts for age, sex, income, occupation, ethnicity, marital and residential status, province, education, smoking, stroke history AND antihypertensive treatment. These coefficients are used as transported conditional associations, not falsely described as age/sex-only estimates or causal effects. Treatment markedly attenuated the association in that paper. Omitting all those additional adjustment variables from the generator is an important unsupported transport assumption. Source BP: seated automated measurements after five minutes rest, normally two readings; third if SBP difference exceeds 10, then last-two mean. (3) Konigorski et al., 2014, doi:10.1186/1753-6561-8-S1-S72, PMC4143670, Methods and Table 3. San Antonio family studies, Mexican-American unrelated subset: 153 with phenotypes, 100 with sequence data. Null copula model Kendall tau=0.578 (SE 0.05; 99% CI 0.449–0.707) for adjusted BP phenotypes. These phenotypes average residuals over up to three exams, after age/sex/smoking adjustment and censored-regression correction for treatment. BMI was NOT adjusted. Source dependence was asymmetric and not Gaussian. This is not the requested single-interview observed-BP residual Pearson correlation.

Derived under assumptions: a Gaussian-copula approximation converts tau to Pearson proxy sin(pi*tau/2), about 0.788. An approximate independent age/sex variance budget removes the specified linear age and sex components from the Brazilian marginal variances. Subtract BMI variance contributions b_s^2*4.6^2 and b_d^2*4.6^2 and covariance b_s*b_d*4.6^2 from that proxy age/sex-adjusted covariance. This yields residual SDs about 15.12/10.18 mmHg and rho about 0.763. This pooled derivation assumes compatible populations/operators, Gaussian dependence, negligible nonlinear reference variance and no reference age-sex-BMI covariance. It is a transparent dependence scenario, NOT a published Pearson estimate. Repeated-exam averaging, treatment correction, sampling uncertainty and BMI adjustment could materially change it.

Explicit unsupported assumptions: decade age probabilities, within-decade uniform integer ages, age-dependent sex probability (roughly 53% women), all conditional BMI age/sex patterns, shifted lognormal shape and limits, BP age slopes/curvatures and female contrasts, constant residual covariance, independent rows, no BMI effect modification. BMI spreads approximate the ELSA scale, not its exact sex-specific SDs. Mean BP curves are centered to the reference age variance and sex mix; curvature allows DBP to peak near age 62 and SBP to continue rising. Widening to ages 20–79 and from civil servants/Chinese screening to a Brazilian laboratory-selected adult distribution is not identifiable from these sources.

Measurement scenario: generate a single baseline interview BP aggregate as if it were the mean of two later seated readings, rounded to 0.5 mmHg, using external cross-sectional scales. No latent untreated BP or longitudinal follow-up BP is substituted. Unknown released final-reading aggregation and baseline timing remain limitations; its measurement error cannot be identified here. Conservative BP/BMI plausibility bounds are modeling choices, NOT claims about the unavailable release dictionary. Rejection of rare implausible pressure pairs can slightly alter nominal associations.

Requested analyses: unweighted OLS separately for SBP and DBP with intercept, age, female, bmi/5; correlate the two residual vectors by Pearson. Nominal conditional BMI slopes above need not equal finite-sample estimates. Nonlinear age effects plus age-dependent BMI can affect linear-age-adjusted slopes and residual correlation. Sensitivity analysis should add age squared; neither regression estimates actual survey coefficients.
